area: Integration paths for SOTA traffic + communication realism in a pure-Python V2X dataset simulator on Windows Server 2022 (SUMO 1.25.0, MOSAIC 25.2, Python 3.12.10, JDK 17)
findings:
All claims below were verified either by live measurement on this host (Windows Server 2022, SUMO 1.25.0 at C:/Users/Administrator/tools/sumo/sumo-1.25.0, MOSAIC 25.2 at C:/Users/Administrator/tools/mosaic, Python 3.12.10) or against primary sources (URLs given).

== (1) SUMO via TraCI / libsumo directly from Python on Windows ==

LOCAL VERIFICATION: sumo.exe 1.25.0 present (MSVC 19.29 release build, SWIG/Parquet/Eigen features); tools/traci and tools/sumolib ship in the Windows zip; no libsumo python module ships in the zip — it comes from PyPI.

PyPI packages (verified via pypi.org JSON): `libsumo` 1.25.0 (released 2025-11-13) has win_amd64 wheels for cp39–cp313 including cp312 (matches local Python 3.12.10); `traci` 1.25.0 is pure-Python (py2.py3-none-any), depends on `sumolib`; `eclipse-sumo` 1.25.0 ships the full SUMO binaries as win_amd64 wheels, so the whole stack is pip-installable and pinnable. Latest line as of 2026-08 is 1.27.1 (traci/libsumo/eclipse-sumo released 2026-06-25) — the project releases synchronized pip packages every version, so maintenance risk is low. Sources: https://pypi.org/project/libsumo/, https://pypi.org/project/traci/, https://pypi.org/project/eclipse-sumo/, https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Libsumo.html

WINDOWS FRICTION FOUND (real, reproducible): `pip install libsumo==1.25.0` pulls dependency `eclipse-sumo` at latest (1.27.1), causing `ImportError: DLL load failed while importing _libsumo` because libsumo's pyd loads SUMO DLLs from the eclipse-sumo package. Fix: pin `eclipse-sumo==1.25.0 sumolib==1.25.0 traci==1.25.0 libsumo==1.25.0`. After pinning, libsumo imports and runs cleanly on this host.

MEASURED PERFORMANCE (this host, 12x12 grid net, 200 m edges, 3000 vehicles over 1200 steps of 1 s, seed 42; ~280 s mean trip duration; benchmark queried getPosition+getSpeed+getAngle for every running vehicle every step = 2,536,473 API calls):
- Pure sumo.exe (no client): 1.59 s wall, SUMO-reported 533,433 UPS, real-time factor 757.
- libsumo in-process (naive per-vehicle getters): 2.14 s → 560 steps/s; only ~35% overhead over pure SUMO despite 2.5 M calls (~1.2 M calls/s).
- TraCI over localhost TCP, naive getters: 37.93 s → 31.6 steps/s (~67 k round-trips/s). 17.7x slower than libsumo.
- TraCI with variable subscriptions (batch retrieval once per step): 6.66 s → 180 steps/s; 5.7x faster than naive TraCI, still 3.1x slower than libsumo.
SUMO docs benchmark context: ~700k UPS single-lane / 240k UPS 4-lane / 80k UPS city grid on an average desktop; no hard limits on network/vehicle count; runtime inversely proportional to step-length (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/FAQ.html). The LibSignal paper independently measured libsumo at ~10x less time cost than TraCI (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10649).

libsumo limitations (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Libsumo.html): sumo-gui does not work with libsumo on Windows; no multiple clients from libsumo itself (but normal TraCI clients can attach to a libsumo instance); subscriptions requiring extra arguments unsupported (except vehicle.getLeader); stricter type checking; must use start() not init()/connect(); `LIBSUMO_AS_TRACI=1` env var makes existing traci scripts run on libsumo unchanged.

DETERMINISM (https://sumo.dlr.de/docs/Simulation/Randomness.html): SUMO is deterministic by default — Mersenne Twister, fixed default seed 23423, separate RNG streams for insertion/flows/driving dynamics/devices; identical results across repeated runs and even across Windows/Linux/macOS with same version+inputs, with documented exceptions: (a) `--device.rerouting.threads` combined with `--weights.random-factor` is non-deterministic; (b) EIDM and Wiedemann car-following models and Proj coordinate transforms may differ across platforms; (c) sub-second step lengths change insertion discretization. TraCI and libsumo drive the same engine, so both inherit this determinism; with multiple TraCI clients you must fix client order via setOrder.

== (2) Eclipse MOSAIC as middleware ==

LOCAL VERIFICATION: MOSAIC 25.2 installed with mosaic.bat (Windows launcher), jars for application/cell/environment/mapping/sns/sumo/ns3/omnetpp ambassadors, plus libsumo-1.24.0.jar (Java binding). The ns-3 and OMNeT++ federates ship ONLY as bash installers + Dockerfiles (bin/fed/ns3/ns3_installer.sh, bin/fed/omnetpp/omnet_installer.sh) — no Windows binaries.

MEASURED: `mosaic.bat -s Barnim` (SUMO + SNS + application + environment + mapping federates) ran end-to-end on this Windows host in 6.0 s total, 2.54 s simulation time for 1000 simulated seconds (RTF 394), exit code 0, using local SUMO 1.25 from PATH. So MOSAIC core + SNS is fully Windows-native (Java 17/21; SUMO 1.0.1–1.25.0 supported by MOSAIC 25.2) (https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/getting_started/).

What MOSAIC adds over direct TraCI: RTI-based time management/synchronization of multiple federates, an Application Simulator (V2X apps as Java classes on vehicles/RSUs with virtual per-unit network addressing, 10.x.0.0 nets), mapping of apps to vehicles, cell simulator (LTE/5G abstraction with capacity/delay models), environment events, and output generators. What it costs a pure-Python project: applications must be written in JAVA — there is no Python application API; your Python code would sit outside the federation, defeating the purpose. Sources: https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/getting_started/, https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/simulators/

SNS fidelity (https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/simulators/network_simulator_sns/): SimpleAdhocTransmissionModel (single logical hop, configured delay) or SophisticatedAdhocTransmissionModel (greedy forwarding + flooding for geo-casts); delay models ConstantDelay/SimpleRandomDelay/GammaRandomDelay; packet loss via a flat `lossProbability` + `maxRetries`; unit-disk `singlehopRadius` (default 509.4 m); `maximumTtl` default 10. NO physical layer: no pathloss/shadowing/fading geometry, no CSMA/CA contention, no channel-load effects — docs explicitly acknowledge speed-over-accuracy. SNS is therefore BELOW the fidelity of a calibrated analytic Python channel model with building geometry; it adds nothing for dataset realism you could not exceed in Python.

MOSAIC ns-3 federate: couples ns-3 3.36.1 with an 802.11p stack; platform list is "GNU/Linux (recommended), FreeBSD, macOS, Microsoft Windows (with WSL or Docker)" — i.e., NOT Windows-native; run via `wsl.exe ./ns3_installer.sh` or Docker (https://eclipse.dev/mosaic/docs/simulators/network_simulator_ns3/). OMNeT++ federate likewise ships only a bash installer/Dockerfile. Note MOSAIC pins old ns-3 3.36.1 (current ns-3 is 3.44+), and OMNeT++ 6.1.

== (3) ns-3 on Windows realistically ==

Official installation guide (https://www.nsnam.org/docs/installation/html/windows.html): ns-3 is NOT compatible with MSVC. Supported Windows routes: (a) Msys2/MinGW64 toolchain — works but second-class: only MinGW64 tested (Clang64 tested unsuccessfully, UCRT untested), emulation features unsupported, packaging friction; (b) WSL2 — the recommended path, "100% code compatibility with Linux," standard Linux install instructions apply; emulation via WSL2 untested/unsupported but plain simulation is fine. ns-3's Python bindings are now cppyy-based and Linux-oriented; driving ns-3 per-step from Windows-native Python would require a custom socket/ZeroMQ bridge across the WSL2 boundary — added latency per step, two runtimes, two RNG domains. ns-3 itself is deterministic given fixed RngSeed/RngRun. Realistic use on this host: offline batch runs inside WSL2 (e.g., ms-van3t, https://github.com/ms-van3t-devs/ms-van3t / https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0140366424000227 — ETSI-compliant 802.11p, LTE-V2X Rel-14, NR-V2X Rel-16 stacks with SUMO mobility) to produce reference PER/latency/CBR curves — not in the per-step dataset-generation loop.

Related: Veins 5.3.1 (https://veins.car2x.org/download/) runs natively on Windows for its base 802.11p DSRC stack (OMNeT++ 5.3–6.1; OMNeT++ ships a Windows MinGW toolchain), but officially supports SUMO only up to 1.22.0, and veins_inet requires WSL on Windows. Veins is a viable native-Windows reference simulator for calibration, with the caveat of running a second SUMO version.

== (4) Pure-Python building blocks ==

GEMV^2: original is MATLAB (Boban et al., IEEE TVT 2014, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6799304 / https://arxiv.org/abs/1305.0124; code at http://vehicle2x.net). Existing ports are C++ only: Artery's gemv2 module (https://github.com/riebl/artery/tree/master/src/artery/inet/gemv2) and ns-3 (https://github.com/rocktale/gemv2-ns3). Two targeted searches found NO maintained Python port — a Python reimplementation is a genuine gap you would fill yourself (~the model is well-documented: LOS/NLOSv/NLOSb link classification from vehicle/building/foliage outlines, deterministic large-scale + geometry-indexed stochastic small-scale variation; validated against urban/suburban/highway/open-space measurements; paper demonstrates city-scale simulation with tens of thousands of vehicles on commodity hardware). R-tree indexing via `shapely.STRtree` makes the geometry tractable in Python.

802.11p PHY/MAC in Python: no maintained pip package exists (searched; MATLAB dominates: MathWorks WLAN Toolbox 802.11p PER example, PhySim-11p https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352711020302934, WiLabV2Xsim for C-V2X). The standard substitute is PHY abstraction: SNR/SINR→PER lookup curves from link-level simulators — methodology in "A Methodology for Abstracting the Physical Layer of Direct V2X Communications Technologies" (Sensors 2022, https://doi.org/10.3390/s22239330) covering both IEEE 802.11p and C-V2X. Generic DSP toolboxes `scikit-commpy` and `komm` exist on PyPI for OFDM/convolutional-coding BER if you want to regenerate curves, but tabulated curves are the pragmatic route. MAC: no Python CSMA/CA library; literature-standard analytic models (Bianchi-style adaptations for 802.11p broadcast, e.g., IET Networks 2018 https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1049/iet-net.2017.0228) or a SimPy-based CSMA/CA process are both feasible in-Python.

OSM building footprints: `osmnx` 2.1.1 (Jan 2025+, actively maintained, Python ≥3.11, geopandas/shapely 2 stack) — `ox.features_from_place(..., tags={"building": True})` for footprints via Overpass; `pyrosm` 0.13.1 (June 2026, Windows wheels cp310–cp314) parses local .osm.pbf extracts into GeoDataFrames offline, with an out-of-core streaming engine for country-scale extracts — better for reproducible pipelines (no Overpass dependency). Both integrate with shapely 2 STRtree for LOS-blockage tests. Sources: https://pypi.org/project/osmnx/, https://pypi.org/project/pyrosm/. Note SUMO's own netconvert/polyconvert can also import OSM building polygons aligned to the SUMO net's local coordinates — convenient because channel geometry then shares the exact mobility coordinate frame.

Optional heavy option: NVIDIA Sionna (https://github.com/NVlabs/sionna) offers ray-traced radio propagation (Sionna RT on Mitsuba/Dr.Jit) but is TensorFlow-based, documented for Linux/macOS, GPU on Windows effectively requires WSL2; overkill and poor Windows fit for this project's runtime loop.

== (5) Hybrid: SUMO mobility + analytic Python channel calibrated to Veins/ns-3 ==

This is the established pattern in the literature and has strong published anchors to calibrate against:
- Obstacle (building) shadowing: Sommer et al., "A Computationally Inexpensive Empirical Model of IEEE 802.11p Radio Shadowing in Urban Environments," WONS 2011 (https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5720204): attenuation = beta*(number of exterior-wall cuts) + gamma*(meters of obstacle interior traversed); Veins' ObstacleControl implements exactly `attenuationPerCut*numCuts + attenuationPerMeter*fraction*totalDistance` (https://github.com/sommer/veins/blob/master/src/veins/modules/obstacle/ObstacleControl.cc) with the measurement-calibrated defaults of 9 dB per wall cut and 0.4 dB per meter used in Veins example configs. Trivially reproducible in Python against pyrosm footprints.
- LOS pathloss: two-ray interference model (Sommer/Dressler, from the same Veins line of work) rather than free-space, plus log-distance with measured exponents for NLOSb.
- Small-scale fading: Nakagami-m with distance-dependent m (the Veins/ns-3 VANET default; m~3 near, m~1 (Rayleigh) far, per Cheng et al. DSRC measurements).
- Link classification + vehicle blockage: GEMV^2 NLOSv knife-edge attenuation over blocking vehicle outlines.
- PHY/MAC: SNR→PER tables per MCS (from PhySim-11p / MathWorks 802.11p PER curves / Sensors 2022 methodology), plus an analytic or SimPy CSMA/CA-with-CBR model to capture channel-load effects.
Everything is NumPy-vectorizable; with STRtree-precomputed obstacle crossings a per-step all-pairs link evaluation for hundreds of vehicles costs milliseconds, keeping the whole loop in one deterministic Python+libsumo process (single seeded numpy.random.Generator + fixed SUMO seed = bit-reproducible datasets). Calibration/validation reference runs come from Veins (native Windows, SUMO<=1.22) or ms-van3t in WSL2, done offline once — not per dataset.

== Cross-path comparison (setup effort / runtime perf / determinism / maintenance risk / Windows friction) ==
1. libsumo direct: hours / 560 steps-s measured, ~35% overhead / deterministic (fixed seed, avoid rerouting-threads+random-factor) / low risk (DLR releases synced pip wheels every version; pin all four packages to one version) / friction only the DLL-pinning gotcha (solved).
2. TraCI direct: hours / 180 steps-s with subscriptions, 32 with naive getters / same determinism, plus sumo-gui debugging works / lowest risk (stable protocol since 2008; TraCI API versioned) / none.
3. MOSAIC+SNS: ~1 day / RTF 394 measured on Barnim / deterministic (randomSeed in scenario config) / medium risk (Java app layer, no Python API; SNS fidelity below your own analytic model) / core is Windows-clean, but you'd write apps in Java.
4. MOSAIC+ns-3/OMNeT++: days / slow (full packet-level) / deterministic per RngRun / high risk on Windows (WSL2 or Docker only, ns-3 pinned to 3.36.1) / high friction.
5. ns-3 standalone WSL2 (ms-van3t): 1–2 days in WSL2 / packet-level, orders slower than analytic / deterministic / medium / high friction for in-loop use, fine for offline calibration.
6. Pure-Python channel (GEMV^2-style + PER tables): ~1–2 weeks to implement+calibrate (no port exists to reuse) / fastest, vectorized / fully deterministic / you own the code — risk is validation, mitigated by the published parameter anchors and offline reference runs.

benchmarks: PDR (packet delivery ratio) vs Tx-Rx distance curves, per environment (urban/suburban/highway) and per link class (LOS/NLOSv/NLOSb) — the primary validation curve in GEMV^2 (IEEE TVT 2014) and Veins papers; compare simulated curves against DSRC measurement campaigns
RMSE of received signal power (dB) between model and drive-test measurements per environment — GEMV^2's headline validation metric (validated in urban/suburban/highway/open-space campaigns)

Building-obstacle attenuation anchors: 9 dB per exterior-wall cut + 0.4 dB per meter of interior traversal (Sommer et al. WONS 2011, calibrated from 802.11p field measurements; Veins ObstacleControl defaults) — reproduce these to inherit Veins-level shadowing realism
Channel Busy Ratio (CBR) vs vehicle density and beacon rate — standard MAC-load realism metric in ETSI DCC / 802.11p literature; validates the CSMA/CA + channel-load abstraction

Packet Inter-Reception time (PIR/IRT) distribution and its tail (e.g., P(PIR > 1 s)) vs distance — standard awareness-continuity metric in C-V2X vs 802.11p comparison studies (e.g., ms-van3t, WiLabV2Xsim papers)
Neighbor Awareness Ratio (fraction of vehicles within range X known to ego within last T) — dataset-level realism metric directly consumable by SCMS/application layers

SNR->PER lookup fidelity: per-MCS PER-vs-SNR curves within ~1 dB of link-level references (PhySim-11p SoftwareX 2020; MathWorks 802.11p PER example; Sensors 2022 22(23):9330 PHY-abstraction methodology for 802.11p and C-V2X)

End-to-end latency distribution (media access + retransmission delay) vs load — what MOSAIC SNS reduces to a Gamma/constant delay model and packet-level simulators produce emergently; compare your analytic delay model to ns-3/Veins reference runs

Traffic realism: GEH statistic < 5 on >= 85% of link counts vs real detector data (UK DMRB/WebTAG calibration standard); speed/travel-time RMSE vs probe data; fundamental-diagram (flow-density) match — applied to SUMO scenario calibration (e.g., LuST-style scenarios)

Runtime/scalability metrics: SUMO UPS (vehicle updates per second; measured 533k UPS on this host, docs cite 80k-700k depending on network) and real-time factor (measured RTF 757 pure SUMO, RTF 394 MOSAIC+SNS Barnim); steps/s with client attached (measured: libsumo 560, TraCI+subscriptions 180, TraCI naive 32)

Reproducibility check: bit-identical dataset hashes across repeated runs with fixed SUMO seed (default 23423) + fixed numpy Generator seed; SUMO docs guarantee cross-platform determinism except EIDM/Wiedemann models and rerouting-threads+random-weight combination
recommendations: 1. PRIMARY PATH — Hybrid, all in one Windows process: SUMO 1.25.0 mobility via libsumo (pip, pinned: libsumo==traci==sumolib==eclipse-sumo==1.25.0 to avoid the verified DLL-mismatch ImportError) + a pure-Python GEMV^2-style channel layer. Measured on this host: 560 steps/s with 3000 vehicles and 2.5M API calls — 17.7x TraCI. Fully deterministic with fixed --seed; keep single-threaded routing or avoid --weights.random-factor.

2. Channel layer design: pyrosm (offline .pbf, reproducible) or netconvert/polyconvert for building footprints in the SUMO coordinate frame; shapely 2 STRtree for LOS-cut queries; Sommer obstacle model (9 dB/cut + 0.4 dB/m) for NLOSb, two-ray interference for LOS, GEMV^2 knife-edge for vehicle blockage (NLOSv), distance-dependent Nakagami-m small-scale fading; per-MCS SNR->PER tables (PhySim-11p / Sensors 2022) + analytic CSMA/CA-CBR model for MAC/load effects. All NumPy-vectorizable; single seeded numpy Generator for bit-reproducible datasets.

3. Calibrate offline, not in-loop: generate reference PDR-vs-distance, CBR, and latency curves once from Veins 5.3.1 (native Windows, but SUMO<=1.22) or ms-van3t/ns-3 in WSL2, and fit/validate the Python channel layer against them (RMSE in dB, PDR curve deviation, PIR tails). Never put ns-3 in the per-step dataset loop on Windows.

4. Keep traci (socket) as a debug/visualization fallback: same scripts via LIBSUMO_AS_TRACI toggle; sumo-gui works only over TraCI on Windows. Use context subscriptions when on TraCI (measured 5.7x faster than naive getters).

5. Deprioritize Eclipse MOSAIC for this project: its core + SNS runs perfectly on this Windows host (verified, RTF 394), but SNS is a unit-disk + configured-delay/loss model with no PHY — lower fidelity than the recommended Python channel layer — and its application layer is Java-only with no Python API. Keep it only as an occasional cross-check harness; its ns-3/OMNeT++ federates need WSL/Docker and pin ns-3 3.36.1.

6. Do not attempt native ns-3 on Windows (MSVC unsupported; MinGW64 path experimental with emulation unsupported). If packet-level ground truth is ever needed continuously, run ms-van3t in WSL2 and bridge via files or ZeroMQ — accept the two-runtime cost.

7. Reproducibility discipline: pin SUMO-stack pip versions to 1.25.0, record SUMO seed + numpy seed + scenario hash in every dataset manifest, and add a CI check that re-running a small scenario produces a bit-identical output hash (SUMO docs guarantee this cross-platform except EIDM/Wiedemann/Proj caveats).
